datatype.name: HistoricalYear
datatype.definition: A calendar year in astronomical numbering, in which 1 CE is 1, 1 BCE is 0 and 2 BCE is -1, so that years before the common era are ordinary integers.

provenance.source: ISO 8601-2:2019, Date and time - Representations for information interchange - Part 2: Extensions
provenance.note: Year zero and negative (expanded) years, by agreement between the communicating parties. The proleptic Gregorian calendar is assumed; an approximate year carries its uncertainty in the paired human-readable period.

datatype.name: UnicodeCodePoint
datatype.definition: A Unicode code point written in the standard U+ notation with four to six uppercase hexadecimal digits.

provenance.ref: Appendix A, Notational Conventions (code points as U+ followed by 4-6 hex digits)

datatype.name: WikidataId
datatype.definition: The identifier of a Wikidata item, the letter Q followed by a positive integer.

provenance.note: A Tier C cross-reference for interoperability (ETHICS.md §2.2); it never supports a fact on its own.

enumeration.name: TraditionVitality
enumeration.definition: Whether a tradition is practised today by a continuing community, is known only historically, or is a modern revival.

provenance.note: A revival is recorded as its own tradition that emergedFrom the historical one; the historical tradition stays HISTORICAL.

value.definition: Practised today by a community that continues it without a break.
No longer practised as a continuous tradition; known from historical and archaeological sources.
A modern reconstruction or revival of a historical tradition.

enumeration.name: Historicity
enumeration.definition: What historical scholarship concludes about whether a figure presented by a tradition existed as a historical person.

provenance.note: The scale records the state of scholarship, not the tradition's belief. Each figure's value is sourced on the individual.

value.definition: Historians broadly agree that the person existed, whatever they conclude about the traditions told of them.
Historians disagree whether, or in what form, the person existed.
Known only from the tradition's own texts; historical method cannot assess the figure's existence.

enumeration.name: PreceptPolarity
enumeration.definition: Whether a precept obliges, recommends, discourages or prohibits the action it concerns.

provenance.note: A four-step scale between obligation and prohibition. Traditions have finer scales of their own, such as the five categories (al-ahkam al-khamsa) of Islamic jurisprudence; those belong to a later sub-domain.

value.definition: The tradition holds the action to be required.
The tradition holds the action to be commendable but not required.
The tradition holds the action to be blameworthy but not forbidden.
The tradition holds the action to be forbidden.

concept.name: BeliefSystem
concept.definition: A coherent body of beliefs, values and practices about what is ultimately real, meaningful or valuable, shared by a community and passed on over time.

provenance.source: ETHICS.md §3.3 (belief systems as a first-class concept)
provenance.note: The identity root (L0 Kind) for religions here and, later, for philosophies and ideologies; a candidate to move to a shared module by issue, never unilaterally.

concept.name: ReligiousTradition
concept.definition: A belief system that a community passes on as a lineage of teachings, practices, narratives and institutions oriented to what it holds sacred or ultimate. A branch of a larger tradition is itself a tradition.

provenance.source: Smart, N. (1996). Dimensions of the Sacred: An Anatomy of the World's Beliefs. University of California Press.
provenance.note: Smart's seven dimensions (doctrinal, narrative, ethical, ritual, experiential, social, material) are the checklist behind the properties below. Defining 'religion' is itself contested; this is a working definition, not a verdict.

property.name: wikidataId
property.definition: The Wikidata item that describes the same tradition.

property.name: vitality
property.definition: Whether the tradition is living, historical or revived.

property.name: emergencePeriod
property.definition: When the tradition emerged as a distinct tradition, in words that keep the uncertainty, for example 'c. 6th-5th century BCE'.

provenance.note: 'Emergence' rather than 'founding': most traditions took shape over a period, and several deny having a beginning in time.

property.name: emergenceStartYear
property.definition: The earliest year of the emergence period, for sorting and querying.

property.name: emergenceEndYear
property.definition: The latest year of the emergence period, for sorting and querying.

property.name: originRegion
property.definition: The region where the tradition emerged, named as it was at the time.

provenance.note: A historical region name, not a modern state: mapping ancient regions to present-day states can take a side in a dispute (ETHICS.md §3.2).

property.name: parentTradition
property.definition: The larger tradition of which this tradition is a branch. A part-whole link between traditions, not inheritance between classes.

provenance.note: A property, not a part_of relation, because L2 individuals carry property values only. Where a placement is contested the individual's notes say so, and rival groupings are scheme claims.

property.name: emergedFrom
property.definition: Traditions this tradition historically arose from, without being a branch of them.

property.name: founders
property.definition: The figures regarded as the tradition's founders, as attributed in the individual's provenance. Empty does not mean that the tradition has none.

provenance.note: Founding is an attribution: a tradition may see a figure as a restorer or a messenger rather than a founder, and historians may weigh the roles differently.

property.name: principalDeities
property.definition: The divine beings at the centre of the tradition's worship, as the tradition conceives them.

property.name: doctrines
property.definition: Central doctrines the tradition teaches.

property.name: ethicalValues
property.definition: Central qualities of character the tradition teaches as good.

property.name: preceptSets
property.definition: Named sets of precepts (commandments, pillars, vows) the tradition transmits.

property.name: sacredTexts
property.definition: Texts the tradition holds as scripture or as authoritative.

property.name: symbols
property.definition: Visual signs widely used to represent the tradition.

concept.name: Deity
concept.definition: A god, goddess or other divine being as conceived within one or more traditions. An individual records a conception; it asserts neither that the being exists nor that conceptions in different traditions coincide.

provenance.source: ETHICS.md §3.3 (belief modelled as belief, with attribution)
provenance.note: An L0 Abstract: the conception. The names a tradition uses for the deity are its labels, in each language and script.

property.name: wikidataId
property.definition: The Wikidata item that describes the same conception.

concept.name: ReligiousFigure
concept.definition: A person or figure who holds a significant place in a tradition's teaching or history, such as a founder, prophet, teacher or reformer, as the tradition presents them.

provenance.note: Not wmoop.nature/Person: a figure is described as a tradition presents them, and its historicity is stated rather than assumed. A future, sourced link may identify a figure with a historical Person.

property.name: historicity
property.definition: What historical scholarship concludes about the figure's existence.

property.name: lifetime
property.definition: The figure's lifetime in words that keep the uncertainty, for example 'c. 563-483 BCE (dates debated)'.

property.name: wikidataId
property.definition: The Wikidata item that describes the same figure.

concept.name: Teaching
concept.definition: A belief, value or rule that a tradition teaches, recorded as that tradition's teaching and not as a claim of WMOOP.

property.name: originalTerm
property.definition: The tradition's own term for the teaching, romanized, for example 'tawhid' or 'anatta'.

provenance.note: Romanization per the whitepaper (IAST for Sanskrit and Pali, ALA-LC for Arabic and Hebrew); native-script forms go in labels.

concept.name: Doctrine
concept.definition: A teaching about what is real or true - the divine, the world, the human condition or its final goal - as a tradition holds it.

concept.name: EthicalValue
concept.definition: A teaching that names a disposition or quality of character that a tradition holds to be good.

concept.name: Precept
concept.definition: A teaching that obliges, recommends, discourages or prohibits a kind of action.

provenance.note: Described in the third person ('abstaining from taking life'), never as an imperative (docs/08-contributing-a-domain.md §3.1).

property.name: polarity
property.definition: Whether the precept obliges, recommends, discourages or prohibits its action.

concept.name: PreceptSet
concept.definition: A named collection of precepts that a tradition passes on as a unit, such as a list of commandments, pillars or vows.

provenance.note: An L0 Collection. The same set may be counted or divided differently by different branches, as the Ten Commandments are.

property.name: traditionalCount
property.definition: How many items the tradition counts in the set.

property.name: precepts
property.definition: The precepts recorded so far as members of the set.

concept.name: SacredText
concept.definition: A text or body of texts that a tradition holds as scripture or as authoritative.

provenance.note: An L0 Abstract (the work), not a physical copy. Canons differ between branches; the individual's notes say so.

property.name: originalLanguages
property.definition: The languages in which the text was composed, as BCP-47 language subtags.

provenance.source: IETF BCP 47, Tags for Identifying Languages

property.name: compositionPeriod
property.definition: When scholars date the composition or compilation of the text, in words that keep the uncertainty.

property.name: wikidataId
property.definition: The Wikidata item that describes the same text.

concept.name: ReligiousSymbol
concept.definition: A visual sign that stands for a tradition, a teaching or a sacred reality for those who use it.

provenance.note: A tradition has symbols, not a logo; an organization's emblem may be a registered trademark. Unicode characters carry no image licence, so they are the default representation.

property.name: unicodeCodePoint
property.definition: The Unicode code point of the character that encodes the symbol, if one exists.

property.name: unicodeName
property.definition: The character's name in the Unicode Character Database.

property.name: wikidataId
property.definition: The Wikidata item that describes the same symbol.

concept.name: ReligiousEvent
concept.definition: A historical occurrence that sources treat as significant in the history of one or more traditions, such as a council, a schism or a revival.

provenance.note: An L0 Perdurant. The traditions involved are referenced; their own accounts of the event may differ and are noted on the individual.

property.name: period
property.definition: When the event happened, in words that keep any uncertainty.

property.name: startYear
property.definition: The year the event began.

property.name: endYear
property.definition: The year the event ended, when it lasted beyond one year.

property.name: place
property.definition: Where the event happened, named as at the time.

property.name: traditions
property.definition: The traditions whose history the event shaped.

property.name: wikidataId
property.definition: The Wikidata item that describes the same event.

concept.name: ReligiousOrganization
concept.definition: An organization through which a community of a religious tradition is governed, such as a church, a union of congregations or a federation of communities.

provenance.note: Eastern Orthodoxy is a tradition; the Romanian Orthodox Church is an organization of that tradition, with a legal name, a legal status and dates of its own.

property.name: tradition
property.definition: The tradition the organization belongs to.

role.name: Cleric
role.definition: The role of a person ordained, appointed or recognised to lead worship, teach or administer rites for a religious organization, such as a priest, minister, imam or rabbi.

provenance.note: An office, so a role on Person by composition [S3]; it records a capacity, not a belief. There is deliberately no Believer or Adherent role: a person's religion is a protected attribute (ETHICS.md §3.1).

property.name: title
property.definition: The title of the office as the organization names it, for example 'preot', 'imam' or 'rabbi'.

relation.name: servesIn
relation.definition: The religious organizations in which the person holds the office.

individual.name: Jesus of Nazareth
individual.definition: The Jewish teacher from Galilee whom Christianity proclaims as the Christ and the Son of God.

provenance.note: Historians of antiquity broadly agree that Jesus existed and was crucified under Pontius Pilate; claims about his divinity are Christian teaching, recorded as such.

individual.name: Muhammad
individual.definition: The Arab religious and political leader whom Islam regards as the final prophet of God.

individual.name: Abraham
individual.definition: The patriarch whom Judaism, Christianity and Islam regard as the father of faith in the one God.

provenance.note: Known only from the scriptures of the three traditions; no independent historical evidence confirms or excludes a historical figure.

individual.name: Moses
individual.definition: The prophet and lawgiver whom Judaism regards as the receiver of the Torah at Sinai, also revered in Christianity and Islam.

provenance.note: No evidence outside the Bible; scholars disagree whether a historical figure lies behind the narratives.

individual.name: Siddhartha Gautama
individual.definition: The teacher from the northern Indian subcontinent known as the Buddha, the 'awakened one', whose teaching is the origin of Buddhism.
individual.value: c. 563-483 BCE or c. 480-400 BCE (dates debated)

provenance.note: His existence is accepted; his dates are not: the older chronology gives c. 563-483 BCE, many scholars now prefer c. 480-400 BCE.

individual.name: Guru Nanak
individual.definition: The first of the ten Sikh Gurus, whose teaching in the Punjab is the origin of Sikhism.

individual.name: Mahavira
individual.definition: The twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara of the present cosmic age in Jain teaching, who reformed and spread the Jain community.
individual.value: traditionally 599-527 BCE; often dated c. 6th-5th century BCE

provenance.note: Jain tradition sees him as the last of a line of teachers, not a founder; it dates him 599-527 BCE, many historians about a century later.

individual.name: Zarathustra
individual.definition: The Iranian prophet traditionally regarded as the founder of Zoroastrianism and the author of the Gathas.
individual.value: dates disputed: c. 628-551 BCE (later tradition) or the 2nd millennium BCE

provenance.note: Treated as a historical prophet; what is disputed is when he lived: c. 628-551 BCE by a date drawn from later Zoroastrian texts, or some time in the second millennium BCE.

individual.name: Bahá'u'lláh
individual.definition: The Iranian religious leader whom the Bahá'í Faith regards as its founder and as the latest messenger of God.

individual.name: Martin Luther
individual.definition: The German theologian whose challenge to Church teaching in 1517 began the Protestant Reformation.

provenance.note: Luther sought to reform the Western Church, not to found a new one; 'founder' of Lutheranism is an attribution by others.

individual.name: John Calvin
individual.definition: The French theologian and Geneva reformer whose theology shaped the Reformed tradition.

individual.name: John Smyth
individual.definition: The English Separatist minister who led the first Baptist congregation, in Amsterdam.

individual.name: Thomas Helwys
individual.definition: The English layman who, with John Smyth, led the first Baptist congregation and brought it back to England.

individual.name: Joseph Smith
individual.definition: The American religious leader whom the Latter Day Saint movement regards as its founding prophet.

individual.name: Laozi
individual.definition: The sage to whom Daoist tradition attributes the Daodejing.

provenance.note: Traditionally an older contemporary of Confucius (6th century BCE); many scholars doubt a single historical author.

individual.name: Holy Trinity
individual.definition: God as conceived in trinitarian Christianity, one God in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

provenance.note: Defined by the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381); nontrinitarian Christian traditions conceive God differently.

individual.name: Allah
individual.definition: God as conceived in Islam, one and unique, without partner or equal.

provenance.note: 'Allah' is the Arabic word for God, used also by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews. Whether the three Abrahamic traditions worship the same God is a theological question WMOOP does not settle; Nostra aetate §3 (1965) states the Catholic view that Muslims adore the one God.

individual.name: YHWH
individual.definition: The God of Israel as conceived in Judaism, whose four-letter name is not pronounced in Jewish practice.

provenance.note: Readers say Adonai ('my Lord') or HaShem ('the Name') instead of the Tetragrammaton; 'Yahweh' is a scholarly reconstruction of its pronunciation.

individual.name: Vishnu
individual.definition: The Hindu god conceived as the preserver of the universe, supreme being in Vaishnavism, worshipped also through avatars such as Krishna and Rama.

individual.name: Shiva
individual.definition: The Hindu god conceived as destroyer and renewer of the universe, supreme being in Shaivism.

individual.name: Ahura Mazda
individual.definition: The supreme, wise and good God of Zoroastrianism.

individual.name: Waheguru
individual.definition: The name most used in Sikhism for the one, formless God.

individual.name: Zeus
individual.definition: The sky god and ruler of the gods in ancient Greek religion.

individual.name: Bible
individual.definition: The Christian scriptures, made of the Old Testament and the New Testament.
individual.value: Hebrew Bible texts across the first millennium BCE; New Testament c. 50-120 CE (scholarly estimates)

provenance.note: The Old Testament canon differs: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include deuterocanonical books that Protestant Bibles omit or set apart.

individual.name: Tanakh
individual.definition: The Hebrew Bible, made of the Torah, the Prophets (Nevi'im) and the Writings (Ketuvim).
individual.value: first millennium BCE; the canon was settled by about the 2nd century CE (debated)

individual.name: Talmud
individual.definition: The body of rabbinic law and discussion made of the Mishnah and the Gemara, in a Jerusalem and a Babylonian version.
individual.value: Mishnah c. 200 CE; Babylonian Talmud completed c. 500-600 CE

provenance.note: Authoritative in Rabbinic Judaism; Karaite Judaism does not accept it.

individual.name: Qur'an
individual.definition: The scripture of Islam, which Muslims hold to be the word of God revealed to Muhammad.
individual.value: 610-632 CE according to Islamic tradition; standard codex c. 650 CE

provenance.note: Islamic tradition dates the revelation 610-632 CE and the standard codex to the caliph Uthman (c. 650 CE).

individual.name: Vedas
individual.definition: The oldest scriptures of Hinduism, four collections of hymns, ritual texts and philosophical teachings transmitted orally.

individual.name: Bhagavad Gita
individual.definition: A Hindu scripture in the Mahabharata, a dialogue in which Krishna instructs the warrior Arjuna.

individual.name: Pali Canon
individual.definition: The Tipitaka, the collection of Buddhist scriptures in Pali preserved by the Theravada tradition.
individual.value: transmitted orally; written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE

individual.name: Guru Granth Sahib
individual.definition: The scripture of Sikhism, which Sikhs regard as their eternal, living Guru.
individual.value: compiled as the Adi Granth in 1604; final recension 1706

individual.name: Avesta
individual.definition: The scriptures of Zoroastrianism, whose oldest part is the Gathas attributed to Zarathustra.
individual.value: oral composition over many centuries BCE (dates disputed); written down in the Sasanian period

individual.name: Book of Mormon
individual.definition: A scripture of the Latter Day Saint movement, which it holds to be an ancient record translated by Joseph Smith.

individual.name: Daodejing
individual.definition: The classic text of Daoism, attributed to Laozi, on the Dao and its power.

individual.name: Latin cross
individual.definition: A cross with a long lower arm, the most widespread symbol of Christianity.

individual.name: Orthodox cross
individual.definition: A cross with a short upper bar and a slanted lower bar, used especially in Slavic Orthodox churches.

provenance.note: Orthodox churches use several forms of the cross; this one is not used by all of them.

individual.name: Star of David
individual.definition: A six-pointed star formed of two triangles, a widely used emblem of Judaism and of the Jewish people.

provenance.note: In wide Jewish use since the 19th century; it also appears on the flag of Israel, a national use distinct from the religious one.

individual.name: Star and crescent
individual.definition: A crescent moon with a star, widely associated with Islam since the Ottoman period.

provenance.note: Many Muslims do not regard it as a religious symbol; Islam has no official symbol.

individual.name: Dharma wheel
individual.definition: An eight-spoked wheel representing the Buddha's teaching and the Noble Eightfold Path.

individual.name: Om
individual.definition: The written form of the sacred syllable Om, central in Hinduism and used also in Buddhism and Jainism.

provenance.note: U+0950 DEVANAGARI OM encodes the same sign as a letter of the Devanagari script; the Sanskrit label uses it.

individual.name: Khanda
individual.definition: The emblem of Sikhism, a double-edged sword within a ring flanked by two curved swords.

provenance.note: The dedicated character, added in Unicode 15.0. Older texts use U+262C ADI SHAKTI, which the Unicode names list annotates as khanda and cross-references to U+1FAAF.

individual.name: Taijitu
individual.definition: The yin-yang diagram of complementary opposites, used in Daoism and in Chinese thought more widely.

individual.name: Torii
individual.definition: The gateway that marks the entrance to a Shinto shrine, used as a symbol of Shinto.

provenance.note: Unicode's character is the map symbol for a Shinto shrine, drawn as a torii.

individual.name: Doctrine of the Trinity
individual.definition: The Christian teaching that God is one being in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

individual.name: Tawhid
individual.definition: The Islamic teaching of the absolute oneness and uniqueness of God.

individual.name: Karma
individual.definition: The teaching that intentional actions have consequences that shape a being's future lives or states.

provenance.note: Shared by Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, which interpret it differently; one individual stands for the shared teaching and each tradition's reading belongs in its own notes.

individual.name: Four Noble Truths
individual.definition: The Buddhist teaching on suffering, its origin, its cessation and the path leading to its cessation.

individual.name: Anatta
individual.definition: The Buddhist teaching that there is no permanent, unchanging self in any being.

individual.name: Agape
individual.definition: Self-giving love for God and neighbour, which Christianity teaches as the greatest of the virtues.

provenance.note: With faith and hope one of the three theological virtues (1 Corinthians 13:13).

individual.name: Metta
individual.definition: Loving-kindness towards all beings, the first of the four sublime attitudes of Buddhist teaching.

provenance.source: Harvey, P. (2000). An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

individual.name: Karuna
individual.definition: Compassion, the wish that beings be free of suffering, one of the four sublime attitudes of Buddhist teaching.

provenance.source: Harvey, P. (2000). An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

individual.name: Ahimsa
individual.definition: Non-violence towards all living beings, central in Jainism and taught also in Hinduism and Buddhism.

individual.name: Seva
individual.definition: Selfless service to others, which Sikhism teaches as a central expression of devotion.

individual.name: Abstaining from taking life
individual.definition: The first of the Five Precepts, the undertaking to abstain from killing living beings.

provenance.source: Harvey, P. (2000). An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

individual.name: Abstaining from taking what is not given
individual.definition: The second of the Five Precepts, the undertaking to abstain from theft.

provenance.source: Harvey, P. (2000). An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

individual.name: Abstaining from sexual misconduct
individual.definition: The third of the Five Precepts, the undertaking to abstain from misconduct concerning sensual pleasures.

provenance.source: Harvey, P. (2000). An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

individual.name: Abstaining from false speech
individual.definition: The fourth of the Five Precepts, the undertaking to abstain from lying.

provenance.source: Harvey, P. (2000). An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

individual.name: Abstaining from intoxicants
individual.definition: The fifth of the Five Precepts, the undertaking to abstain from intoxicating drink and drugs that cloud the mind.

provenance.source: Harvey, P. (2000). An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

individual.name: Shahada
individual.definition: The first pillar of Islam, the profession that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the messenger of God.

individual.name: Salat
individual.definition: The second pillar of Islam, the ritual prayer performed five times a day.

individual.name: Zakat
individual.definition: The third pillar of Islam, the obligatory giving of a share of one's wealth to those in need.

individual.name: Sawm
individual.definition: The fourth pillar of Islam, fasting from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan.

individual.name: Hajj
individual.definition: The fifth pillar of Islam, the pilgrimage to Mecca, due once in a lifetime from every Muslim who is able to make it.

individual.name: Five Precepts
individual.definition: The basic ethical undertakings of lay Buddhists.

provenance.source: Harvey, P. (2000). An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

individual.name: Five Pillars of Islam
individual.definition: The five acts that Islam holds obligatory for every Muslim who is able to perform them.

provenance.note: The canonical Sunni list; Shia traditions arrange the obligatory practices in their own lists.

individual.name: Ten Commandments
individual.definition: The Decalogue, the precepts given in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5, held in Judaism and Christianity.

provenance.note: Jewish, Catholic and Lutheran, and Orthodox and Reformed traditions divide the same text into ten in different ways, so the individual precepts are left for a later PR that models each numbering as a scheme.

individual.name: Christianity
individual.definition: The tradition centred on the life, teaching, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth, whom it proclaims as the Christ.

provenance.note: Christianity emerged within Second Temple Judaism; the 'emergedFrom' link points to Judaism as a whole, of which Rabbinic Judaism is the other heir.

individual.name: Catholicism
individual.definition: The branch of Christianity in communion with the Bishop of Rome, comprising the Latin Church and the Eastern Catholic Churches.
individual.value: Latin and Greek Christianity grew apart over centuries; the schism of 1054 is the conventional date

provenance.note: Catholicism holds that it continues the Church of the apostles without a new beginning; 1054 is the conventional date of its separation from Eastern Orthodoxy.

individual.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
individual.definition: The branch of Christianity formed by the autocephalous churches in communion with the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople.
individual.value: Greek and Latin Christianity grew apart over centuries; the schism of 1054 is the conventional date

provenance.note: Like Catholicism, Orthodoxy holds that it continues the apostolic Church; 1054 is a conventional, not a founding, date.

individual.name: Oriental Orthodoxy
individual.definition: The branch of Christianity formed by the churches that did not accept the Council of Chalcedon, including the Coptic, Armenian, Syriac and Ethiopian churches.
individual.value: after the Council of Chalcedon, 451 CE

individual.name: Protestantism
individual.definition: The branch of Christianity that arose from the 16th-century Reformation, stressing the authority of scripture and salvation by grace through faith.
individual.value: Holy Roman Empire and the Swiss Confederacy

individual.name: Lutheranism
individual.definition: The Protestant tradition that follows the theology of Martin Luther as set out in the Lutheran confessions.
individual.value: Electorate of Saxony, Holy Roman Empire

individual.name: Reformed Christianity
individual.definition: The Protestant tradition shaped by Zwingli, Calvin and the Reformed confessions, also called Calvinism.

individual.name: Anglicanism
individual.definition: The tradition of the Church of England and the churches in communion with the Archbishop of Canterbury.
individual.value: 16th century CE, from the English break with Rome in 1534

provenance.note: Placed under Protestantism by common reference usage; many Anglicans describe their church as both Catholic and Reformed, a 'middle way', and reject the plain label Protestant.

individual.name: Baptists
individual.definition: The Protestant tradition that baptizes believers on their profession of faith, usually by immersion, and governs each congregation independently.
individual.value: English Separatist exiles in Amsterdam, Dutch Republic

individual.name: Pentecostalism
individual.definition: The Protestant tradition that stresses baptism in the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues and healing.
individual.value: 1901-1906 CE (Topeka, then the Azusa Street Revival)

individual.name: Adventism
individual.definition: The Protestant tradition that expects the imminent second coming of Christ, the largest body of which is the Seventh-day Adventist Church.
individual.value: from the Millerite movement of the 1840s; the Seventh-day Adventist Church was organised in 1863
New England and New York, United States

individual.name: Latter Day Saint movement
individual.definition: The tradition begun by Joseph Smith, which holds that he restored the original church of Christ; its largest body is The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

group.label: Mișcarea Sfinților din Zilele din Urmă

provenance.note: Not a Protestant tradition: it teaches a restoration, not a reformation. Placed under Christianity by its own self-understanding and by common religious-studies usage; the Catholic Church, the Orthodox churches and many Protestant churches regard it as outside historic Christianity because it rejects the Nicene doctrine of the Trinity. The church asks to be called by its full name rather than 'Mormon'.

individual.name: Islam
individual.definition: The tradition of submission to the one God as taught in the Qur'an and the example of Muhammad, whom it regards as the final prophet.

provenance.note: Islam regards itself as the original religion of all the prophets, restored through Muhammad, not as a new religion with a founder; historians date its emergence to 7th-century Arabia. In Romanian, 'islamism' also names political Islamism, so 'islam' is the clearer label.

individual.name: Sunni Islam
individual.definition: The largest branch of Islam, which recognises the first four caliphs as rightful successors of Muhammad and follows the sunna as transmitted by the community.
individual.value: from the succession dispute after 632 CE; consolidated over the following centuries

individual.name: Shia Islam
individual.definition: The branch of Islam which holds that leadership of the community passed from Muhammad to Ali and his descendants, the Imams.
individual.value: from the succession dispute after 632 CE; consolidated over the following centuries

individual.name: Judaism
individual.definition: The tradition of the Jewish people, centred on the covenant with the one God and on the Torah, written and oral.
individual.value: Israelite religion of the Iron Age (from c. 1000 BCE); Rabbinic Judaism after 70 CE
Ancient Israel and Judah, southern Levant

provenance.note: Judaism traces itself to the covenant with Abraham and the revelation to Moses; historians trace it to Israelite religion of the Iron Age and to Rabbinic Judaism after the destruction of the Second Temple (70 CE).

individual.name: Orthodox Judaism
individual.definition: The branch of Judaism that holds the written and oral Torah to be divinely given and Jewish law binding in full.
individual.value: 19th century CE, as a named movement

provenance.note: Orthodox Jews see their practice as continuous with traditional Judaism; the name and the self-conscious movement date from the 19th-century response to Reform.

individual.name: Conservative Judaism
individual.definition: The branch of Judaism that holds Jewish law binding while seeing it as developing historically; called Masorti outside North America.
individual.value: German states and the United States

individual.name: Reform Judaism
individual.definition: The branch of Judaism that regards Jewish law as open to change and stresses its ethical teaching; also called Progressive or Liberal Judaism.

individual.name: Bahá'í Faith
individual.definition: The tradition founded by Bahá'u'lláh, which teaches the oneness of God, of religion and of humanity.
individual.value: 1863 CE (Bahá'u'lláh's declaration), from the Bábí movement of 1844

provenance.note: It arose from the Bábí movement within Shia Islam, which is why 'emergedFrom' links it to Shia Islam; Bahá'ís regard it as an independent religion, not a branch of Islam.

individual.name: Hinduism
individual.definition: The family of traditions of the Indian subcontinent that look to the Vedas and to dharma, called by many adherents Sanatana Dharma, the eternal order.
individual.value: no single beginning; Vedic roots c. 1500-500 BCE, classical synthesis c. 500 BCE - 300 CE

provenance.note: No founder and no single creed. Theism claims below are one per strand, all normal rank: none of them is 'the' answer.

individual.name: Vaishnavism
individual.definition: The Hindu tradition that worships Vishnu, or his avatars Krishna and Rama, as the supreme God.

individual.name: Shaivism
individual.definition: The Hindu tradition that worships Shiva as the supreme God.

individual.name: Buddhism
individual.definition: The tradition based on the teaching of the Buddha on suffering, its cause and the path to liberation from it.
individual.value: c. 5th century BCE (dates of the Buddha debated)
Gangetic plain, northern Indian subcontinent (Magadha and Kosala)

provenance.note: Gods (devas) appear in Buddhist cosmology but are neither creators nor the source of liberation, hence the non-theistic classification.

individual.name: Theravada
individual.definition: The branch of Buddhism that preserves the Pali Canon, predominant in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia.

individual.name: Mahayana
individual.definition: The branch of Buddhism centred on the bodhisattva path, predominant in East Asia.

individual.name: Vajrayana
individual.definition: The tantric branch of Buddhism, predominant in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia.

provenance.note: Counted as a third vehicle by some, and as a form of Mahayana by others; placed under Buddhism here, with the Mahayana reading recorded in this note.

individual.name: Jainism
individual.definition: The tradition of liberation of the soul through non-violence, ascetic discipline and right knowledge, taught by the Tirthankaras.
individual.value: historically c. 6th-5th century BCE; eternal in Jain teaching

provenance.note: Jains regard their teaching as eternal, renewed by 24 Tirthankaras in each cosmic age; historians place Mahavira, the 24th, in the 6th-5th century BCE. No creator god, hence the non-theistic classification.

individual.name: Sikhism
individual.definition: The tradition founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab, centred on devotion to the one God and on the teaching of the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib.

provenance.note: Older accounts described it as a synthesis of Hinduism and Islam; Sikh scholarship rejects that reading, so no 'emergedFrom' link is recorded.

individual.name: Zoroastrianism
individual.definition: The tradition of ancient Iran based on the teaching of Zarathustra, centred on Ahura Mazda and the struggle between truth and falsehood.
individual.value: dates disputed, between c. 1500 and c. 500 BCE

individual.name: Daoism
individual.definition: The Chinese tradition of living in harmony with the Dao, including both philosophical texts and an organised religion with priests, temples and deities.
individual.value: philosophical texts from c. 4th century BCE; organised religion from the 2nd century CE

provenance.note: Whether 'philosophical' Daoism (daojia) and 'religious' Daoism (daojiao) are one tradition is debated; this individual stands for the religion and its texts.

individual.name: Shinto
individual.definition: The indigenous tradition of Japan, centred on the worship of kami at shrines.
individual.value: prehistoric roots; named and systematised from c. 6th century CE

provenance.note: No founder; it was named and systematised in contrast with Buddhism from about the 6th century CE.

individual.name: Ancient Greek religion
individual.definition: The religion of the ancient Greek world, centred on the worship of the Olympian gods, heroes and local deities in public and household cult.
individual.value: Bronze Age roots; public cult ended in the late 4th century CE

provenance.note: Modern Hellenic polytheism is a revival and, if added, a separate REVIVED tradition that emergedFrom this one.

individual.name: First Council of Nicaea
individual.definition: The first ecumenical council of the Christian church, which issued the original Nicene Creed against Arianism.

group.label: Sinodul I Ecumenic de la Niceea

individual.name: Council of Chalcedon
individual.definition: The ecumenical council that defined Christ as one person in two natures, a definition the Oriental Orthodox churches did not accept.

group.label: Sinodul al IV-lea Ecumenic de la Calcedon

individual.name: East-West Schism
individual.definition: The break of communion between the churches of Rome and Constantinople, conventionally dated to the mutual excommunications of 1054.
individual.value: 1054 CE (conventional date of a gradual separation)

provenance.note: Historians see a gradual estrangement rather than one event; the excommunications were lifted in 1965.

individual.name: Hijrah
individual.definition: The migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina, from which the Islamic calendar counts its years.

individual.name: Succession dispute after Muhammad
individual.definition: The dispute over the leadership of the Muslim community after Muhammad's death, from which the Sunni and Shia branches developed.

group.label: Disputa succesiunii după moartea lui Mahomed

provenance.note: Sunni and Shia accounts of the succession differ; the branches took their full shape over the following centuries.

individual.name: Ninety-five Theses
individual.definition: Martin Luther's propositions against the sale of indulgences, conventionally taken as the start of the Protestant Reformation.
individual.value: Wittenberg, Electorate of Saxony, Holy Roman Empire

provenance.note: Traditionally dated 31 October 1517; whether Luther posted them on the church door at Wittenberg is debated.

individual.name: Organization of the Church of Christ
individual.definition: The formal organization of Joseph Smith's church, the beginning of the Latter Day Saint movement as an institution.

provenance.source: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Church History in the Fulness of Times
provenance.note: The church's own account places the meeting in the home of Peter Whitmer Sr. at Fayette, New York; 'place' stays at the regional level.

individual.name: Declaration of Bahá'u'lláh
individual.definition: Bahá'u'lláh's announcement to his companions in the Garden of Ridvan that he was the messenger foretold by the Báb.
individual.value: Garden of Ridvan, Baghdad, Ottoman Empire

individual.name: Azusa Street Revival
individual.definition: The revival led by William J. Seymour in Los Angeles that spread Pentecostalism worldwide.

individual.name: Romanian Orthodox Church
individual.definition: The autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church of Romania, a patriarchate since 1925.

provenance.source: Legea nr. 489/2006 privind libertatea religioasă și regimul general al cultelor
Basilica.ro, news agency of the Romanian Patriarchate
provenance.ref: Synodal act on 140 years of autocephaly and the centenary of the Patriarchate
provenance.note: Autocephaly recognised on 25 April 1885; raised to a patriarchate on 4 February 1925. Neither is a founding date, so foundingDate stays empty.

individual.name: Baptist Union of Romania
individual.definition: The union of Baptist churches that holds the status of a recognised religious denomination in Romania.

group.label: Uniunea Bisericilor Creștine Baptiste din România

individual.value: Uniunea Bisericilor Creștine Baptiste din România

provenance.source: Legea nr. 489/2006 privind libertatea religioasă și regimul general al cultelor

provenance.note: Listed there as 'Cultul Creștin Baptist – Uniunea Bisericilor Creștine Baptiste din România'.

individual.name: Pentecostal Union of Romania
individual.definition: The Pentecostal union, the Apostolic Church of God, that holds the status of a recognised religious denomination in Romania.

group.label: Uniunea Penticostală – Biserica lui Dumnezeu Apostolică din România

individual.value: Uniunea Penticostală – Biserica lui Dumnezeu Apostolică din România

provenance.source: Legea nr. 489/2006 privind libertatea religioasă și regimul general al cultelor

provenance.note: Listed there as 'Cultul Creștin Penticostal – Biserica lui Dumnezeu Apostolică din România'.

individual.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church in Romania
individual.definition: The Seventh-day Adventist church that holds the status of a recognised religious denomination in Romania.

group.label: Biserica Creștină Adventistă de Ziua a Șaptea din România
Biserica Adventistă de Ziua a Șaptea din România

individual.value: Biserica Creștină Adventistă de Ziua a Șaptea din România

provenance.source: Legea nr. 489/2006 privind libertatea religioasă și regimul general al cultelor

provenance.note: Listed there as 'Biserica Adventistă de Ziua a Șaptea din România'.

individual.name: Assemblies of God in Romania
individual.definition: The Pentecostal Assemblies of God in Romania, recognised as a religious denomination in 2024, the nineteenth under Law no. 489/2006.
